summary: A global bond sell-off pushed the 10-year US Treasury yield to 5.35%, its highest level since 2002.
Drones sank two cargo ships in NATO members' economic zones for the first time, killing at least two sailors.
Hackers hijacked three country-code domains to obtain counterfeit security certificates for Google and other big services.
Paramount closed its $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery; the combined company is now called Skydance.

stories.headline: Bond sell-off pushes US yields to 2002 highs
stories.dek: The 10-year Treasury hit 5.35% as traders braced for a $39 billion auction.
stories.whatHappened: US Treasury yields climbed again on Wednesday. The benchmark 10-year note rose nearly 8 basis points to 5.35%, its highest level since 2002, and the 30-year bond reached 5.724%, also a 24-year high. The Financial Times reports French, Italian and UK government bonds also came under pressure.
stories.whyItMatters: Treasury yields are the baseline for borrowing costs, from mortgages and car loans to company debt. Today's auction tests whether investors will buy at these levels or demand an even bigger premium.
stories.explainSimply: Think of the US government as the world's biggest borrower. When lenders get nervous, they ask for more interest before they'll lend. That higher rate trickles down to everyone else's loans, like a price rise at the wholesale market showing up on every shop's shelf.
stories.background:
Yields have been rising amid concerns about inflation, government debt levels and term risk, the extra return investors want for lending over long periods. This week the Treasury is selling a large batch of debt: $58 billion of 3-year notes on Tuesday, $39 billion of 10-year notes today and $22 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday.

The pressure isn't only American. The FT reports volatile trading in French, Italian and UK government bonds, while France's central bank chief said ECB intervention wasn't needed to ease the rout. CNBC notes oil prices moved higher as yields rose.

stories.headline: Drones sink cargo ships inside NATO waters
stories.dek: Two ships sank and a third burned in attacks Bulgaria called a blatant violation of international law.
stories.whatHappened: Drones sank two cargo ships and damaged a third in the exclusive economic zones of NATO member countries, the first time that has happened, killing at least two sailors. The Togo-flagged Alfa Watan sank and the Palau-flagged Able was set ablaze about 80 miles off Bulgaria on October 6, according to the Associated Press.
stories.whyItMatters: Strikes inside NATO members' economic zones mark a notable escalation in attacks on Black Sea shipping. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev called it "an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone."
stories.explainSimply: An economic zone is like a country's front yard at sea: it doesn't own the water outright, but it has special rights there. These attacks are like a neighbour's fight spilling over the fence. It isn't your fight, but now it's happening on your property.
stories.background:
Commercial shipping in the Black Sea has increasingly come under attack during Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and Russia has been accused of carrying out "hybrid warfare" incidents across Europe. Until now, those attacks had not sunk ships inside NATO members' economic zones.

The ships were hit by multiple sea and aerial drones. A Bulgarian ferry evacuated the Able's 18 crew members, and two severely injured sailors were flown to hospital in Varna. The fate of the Alfa Watan's crew was not immediately known.

stories.headline: Hackers forge security certificates for Google
stories.dek: Attackers hijacked three country domains to mint fake HTTPS credentials for major services.
stories.whatHappened: Attackers took over three country-code top-level domains (.gh, .sl and .as) and changed DNS records for selected domains inside them, Google said Tuesday. That let them obtain unauthorized TLS certificates for several Google domains and for other leading brands and widely used online services.
stories.whyItMatters: A counterfeit certificate can let an attacker impersonate a trusted website. This attack got in through weaknesses at small domain registries rather than at the big companies themselves.
stories.explainSimply: Imagine an ID office that checks who you are by mailing a code to your home address. The hackers hijacked the street's mail delivery, received the code, and walked out with a real ID card in someone else's name.
stories.background:
TLS certificates are the cryptographic credentials behind the padlock in your browser. Each one binds a domain name such as google.com to a public key, while the matching private key stays with the site's operator, so visitors can check they're talking to the real site.

Certificates are issued after automated checks that the requester controls the domain. By modifying the authoritative DNS records inside the hijacked domains, the attackers passed those checks.

keyPlayers.role: Disclosed the attack on Tuesday; several of its domains were targeted

stories.headline: ChatGPT text gets a hidden watermark in the EU
stories.dek: OpenAI turns it on by default in Europe to meet the AI Act. Elsewhere it stays off unless you switch it on.
stories.whatHappened: OpenAI will automatically watermark text generated with ChatGPT in the European Union. The feature will also be offered in other regions, but switched off by default. OpenAI's method, called textGrain, hides patterns in word choices that readers can't notice but a detector with the right key can.
stories.whyItMatters: Europe now requires AI-generated content to be detectably marked, but no watermark is fully reliable yet. Ars Technica says this one is likely easy to get around, like existing approaches.
stories.explainSimply: It's like a baker who always arranges the sprinkles in a secret pattern. You'd never notice, but someone with the pattern key can tell which cakes came from that bakery. Shuffle the sprinkles, though, and the signature disappears.
stories.background:
The EU AI Act took effect in August and requires content produced by AI models to be marked in a way another tool can detect. Approaches already exist, including Google's SynthID and the C2PA project, but they are relatively easy for someone with basic know-how to get around.

OpenAI's textGrain is proprietary, and the company has published a technical paper explaining how it works. Separately, Google on Tuesday opened its SynthID Detector site to everyone, letting anyone check whether an image, video or audio clip was made with AI.

stories.headline: Finland halts work on two Google data centres
stories.dek: Regulators cite forest clearance, a month after Google's record €13bn pledge.
stories.whatHappened: Finland's Licensing and Supervision Agency (LVV) ordered Google to suspend building work at two planned data-centre sites, in Muhos and Kajaani, until environmental impact assessments are complete. It follows concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
stories.whyItMatters: The sites are part of Google's record €13bn ($15bn) Finnish investment, its largest single investment in Europe. The pause shows environmental rules can slow the race to build AI infrastructure.
stories.explainSimply: It's like clearing your garden for an extension before the council has approved the plans. The council doesn't cancel the extension. It just tells you to put the shovel down until the paperwork is done.
stories.background:
Google announced the €13bn investment in Finland less than a month ago. Finland has emerged as a key location for data centres during the AI boom.

The LVV issued its notice on Tuesday to Google subsidiary Tuike Finland Oy. The agency said work at one site was carried out without a mandatory environmental impact assessment. The suspension covers tree removal, excavation, quarrying, soil moving and road building.

stories.headline: Paramount and Warner close $111B merger as Skydance
stories.dek: Two of Hollywood's biggest studios, plus HBO Max, Paramount+, CBS and CNN, are now one company.
stories.whatHappened: Paramount Skydance completed its $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery after Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan rejected a last-ditch effort to block it. The combined company, called Skydance and led by CEO David Ellison, brings together two major studios, Paramount+, HBO Max, CBS, CNN and sports brands including TNT Sports.
stories.whyItMatters: Fewer, bigger media companies now control more of what people watch. Ars Technica reports HBO Max, Paramount+ and Discovery+ will be unified into one service, which could lead to higher prices.
stories.explainSimply: Picture two big supermarket chains merging. You get one giant store with almost everything under one roof, but fewer rival stores nearby to keep prices in check.
stories.background:
The new company takes the name of Skydance, a firm Paramount bought in a separate deal last year. David Ellison's long-anticipated deal to combine Paramount-Skydance with Warner Bros. Discovery faced months of public protests.

California and 11 other states sued to stop it, and in July US District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín ruled the combination would likely reduce competition substantially and violate antitrust laws. The deal ultimately cleared its legal and regulatory challenges in the US and Europe.

stories.headline: Mistral unveils 'le Chonk', a trillion-parameter open model
stories.dek: France's AI champion says Mistral Large 4 ranks among the best open models in the world.
stories.whatHappened: Mistral unveiled Mistral Large 4 (ML4), nicknamed "le Chonk", on Tuesday. The French company says the 1-trillion-parameter model ranks among the best open models in the world and is particularly strong at cyber, coding, manufacturing, finance and multimodal tasks.
stories.whyItMatters: The most capable open AI models have so far been Chinese, and access to them has become a flashpoint in the US–China tech race. This is Europe's strongest bid yet to compete.
stories.explainSimply: An open model is like a recipe published in full, instead of a dish you can only order at one restaurant. Anyone can cook it, tweak it and serve it in their own kitchen, which is why it matters who publishes the best recipes.
stories.background:
Western developers are racing to close the gap with Chinese companies in open-weight and open-source AI.

Mistral, long considered Europe's only answer to OpenAI and Anthropic, raised a €3 billion ($3.4 billion) Series D in September at a €21 billion valuation, cementing it as one of the best-funded AI startups in the region.

stories.headline: Chemistry Nobel solves the mystery of life's mirror molecules
stories.dek: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai explained how life ends up using just one 'hand' of a molecule.
stories.whatHappened: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for discovering non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Their work explains how life's preference for one mirror-image form of a molecule can emerge spontaneously.
stories.whyItMatters: The Nobel Committee called the reactions "spectacular" and said the discoveries have been decisive for chemists who design reactions to make pharmaceuticals.
stories.explainSimply: Your left and right hands are mirror images, but a left glove won't fit your right hand. Molecules work the same way, and life only ever wears one of the gloves. Kagan and Soai showed how a tiny head start for one hand can snowball until it takes over.
stories.background:
Many molecules come in two forms that are mirror images of each other. Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, are one example, yet living organisms on Earth only function with one of the two forms.

Why life favours one form, a property called homochirality, was a chemical mystery more than a century old. "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution," said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.

stories.headline: SpaceX looks to raise $40bn to buy Nvidia chips
stories.dek: A blockbuster debt deal shows how much money is pouring into AI hardware.
stories.whatHappened: SpaceX is looking to raise $40bn to buy Nvidia chips, according to the Financial Times, which describes it as a blockbuster debt deal.
stories.whyItMatters: The FT calls it the latest sign of the vast spending on chips and other infrastructure underpinning AI. The full story is behind the FT's paywall, so the deal's terms aren't included here.
stories.explainSimply: It's like taking out a huge loan not to buy a house, but to buy the bricks. Chips are the raw material every AI system is built from.
stories.background: It comes amid a wider rush of money into AI computing. TechCrunch reports Nvidia-backed Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation ahead of a planned 2027 IPO, and CNBC reports China's DeepSeek is weighing upsizing its funding round to as much as $14.9 billion.

stories.headline: Kenya quarantines contacts after its first Ebola case
stories.dek: The patient travelled from DR Congo through Uganda before dying in Nairobi.
stories.whatHappened: Ten people who came into contact with a man who died of Ebola in Kenya have been quarantined, and health officials are trying to trace 57 other contacts. The patient travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo and died in hospital in Nairobi on Monday. It is Kenya's first-ever Ebola case.
stories.whyItMatters: The patient was sick for a month yet crossed several borders undetected, raising concerns about screening measures in the region.
stories.explainSimply: Contact tracing is like finding everyone who touched a wet-paint sign. You list every person the patient met, then watch them closely so any new case is caught before it spreads further.
stories.background:
According to the head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, drove to Uganda and eventually flew to Kenya without his illness being detected.

Kenyan health officials have quarantined 10 contacts and are tracing 57 more.
